attributes.title: Level 7

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you draw an irregular shape that will fit well with the torch and fireplace sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might pixels be arranged to create a flame image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what the overall shape of a flame might look like. Have them tinker with the placement of different pixels to show an irregular shape. In the next steps, additional frames will be added to show the flame moving through different images, adding movement to the sprite.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by creating a flame image asset to add to the torch and fireplace sprites!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, then create a new flameImage asset. 


Use orange (4) to draw a flame on the canvas. The flame image should only be 5 or 6 pixels wide, and less than 16 pixels tall. Use an irregular shape that depicts what a flame might look like in real life, like this:

steps.hints: ❓ Did you duplicate the first frame in the flameAnim animation asset, then update the image to make it look slightly different?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What button should be used to duplicate a frame in the animation paint editor?

❓ Where might a highlight be placed in the second frame of the flameAnim animation asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can select the frame they’d like to duplicate in the animation paint editor, then click Duplicate Current Frame to create a copy of the image.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what a flame might look like in real life. Typically, the hottest part of the flame can be found in the middle of the flame, towards the bottom. Have the ninja use this information to draw a highlight, representing the hottest part of the flame, on the image.
steps.instructions:
Create an animation asset to animate the flame image!


Use Ctrl + A to select, then copy the entire flame image. Create a new flameAnim animation asset then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor. 


Duplicate the first frame by clicking . In the new frame, use Ctrl + A to select the entire flame. Use the horizontal flip tool to switch the orientation of the flame. 


Use yellow (5) to add a highlight, showing the inner part of the flame. Then use the erase and paint tools to update the rest of the flame, making it look slightly different than the first frame.


Click in the top right corner to preview the animation as it cycles through the 2 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you tinker with the Interval Between Frames (ms) value in the preview animation screen on the upper right to see the flames move faster or slower?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might each frame be modified in the flameAnim animation asset to create 5 distinct images?

❓ Where might pixels be added, removed, and rearranged in each frame?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider how a flame might move in real life. As needed, they may look up an example of this for a visual to model their pixel art drawing off of. Have the ninja add, remove, and rearrange pixels to show the moving and unpredictable nature of a flame across the 5 images.
steps.instructions:
Add additional frames to the flame animation asset!


Duplicate the second frame image in the flameAnim animation asset. In the new frame, use the erase, paint, and horizontal flip tools to make the third image look slightly different than the one before. 


Consider how a flame might move in real life; showing where it might flow between sides, how crackling might cause pixels break off, and how the size of the inner and outer flames might decrease. 


Repeat this 2 more times, so that there are 5 flame images in total.


Click to preview the animation as it cycles through the 5 frames of still images.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use different values as the frameInterval arguments in all 3 runImageAnimation functions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might different frameInterval values be used in each of the runImageAnimation functions?

❓ Do the flame sprites appear in the expected positions with the torch and fireplace sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use different frameInterval values in each of the runImageAnimation functions to cause the torch and fireplace sprites to animate at different rates. Prompt the ninja to consider why it might be useful to animate different sprites at different speeds.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out the positioning of the flame sprites. If the flame sprite does not appear in front of the fireplace sprite, encourage the ninja to consider the sequence or z-property of each sprite to position them correctly. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Use the flame animation asset to animate the torch and fireplace sprites on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor and notice that there is already code that places a left torch, a right torch, and a fireplace on the screen.


Add 3 flame sprites to the project, setting their positions strategically so that the flames appear as expected when the project is run. 


Code each sprite to animate continuously using the flameAnim asset. Use different frameInterval values in each function, so that the flames move at different speeds. 


Click ▶ to see the animated flame sprites on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use 2 different colors to draw a pendulum cable and pendulum bob in the clockAnim animation asset?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What colors might be used to draw the pendulum cable and bob?

❓ What other frames might be added to the clockAnim animation asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they might use complementary colors to create a sharp contrast between the pendulum and the rest of the clock’s body. This will allow the pendulum animation to appear more clearly on the sprite.

💡 In the next steps, frames will be updated to show the pendulum changing position and swinging from one side to the other.
steps.instructions:
Add a pendulum to the clock image asset to create a grandfather clock!


In the Assets menu, open the clockImage asset. Use Ctrl + A to select, then copy the entire clock image. 


Create a new clockAnim animation asset. Resize the canvas to 16 x 32, then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor. 


Duplicate the first frame by clicking .


In the first frame, draw a vertical line in the center of the purple rectangle on the lower part of the clock, representing the cable that swings the pendulum. Then use the circle tool in a different color to draw the pendulum bob at the bottom of the cable, representing the weight that swings back and forth.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the marquee and horizontal flip tools to create left and right swinging frames in the clockAnim asset?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might pixels be arranged in a staircase effect, to show the pendulum swinging to the left?

❓ What section should be selected by the marquee tool to create a right swinging pendulum frame?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider how they might create a diagonal line to show the pendulum cable swinging towards the left. They should consider the number of pixels within each “step” of the pendulum cable and how to gradually move them to the bottom left corner.

💡 Make sure the ninja uses the marquee tool to select only the purple rectangle on the clock. Once selected, the ninja can use the horizontal flip tool to flip the pendulum to be right facing.
steps.instructions:
Create a swinging pendulum using multiple frames in the clock animation asset!


In the frame without a pendulum, draw a pendulum that appears to be swinging to the left inside the purple rectangle. 


Instead of having a straight vertical line to represent the pendulum cable, arrange pixels in a staircase effect from the top center towards the bottom left of the purple rectangle. 


Draw the pendulum bob so that it appears below the new placement of the cable and so the left half appears hidden behind the clock.


Duplicate the left swinging pendulum frame. Use the marquee tool to select only the purple rectangle that contains the pendulum. Use the horizontal flip tool to flip the pendulum inside the purple rectangle to create a right swinging pendulum frame.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with the Interval Between Frames (ms) value in the preview animation screen on the upper right to see the pendulum swing faster or slower?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What order should the frames in the clockAnim asset be placed in?

❓ What happens when the animation is run in the preview window?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja reorder the frames in the clockAnim asset so that the pendulum swings to the left, returns to the middle, swings to the right, then returns to the middle.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test the animation in the preview window, to make sure it moves as expected. Prompt them to tinker with the Interval Between Frames value to test whether the animation should run at a slow or fast speed.
steps.instructions:
Rearrange the frames in the animation asset to match the realistic movement of a pendulum!


Duplicate the frame showing the straight pendulum so that there are 4 frames total. 


Reorder the frames so that the pendulum is shown swinging to the left, returning to the center, swinging to the right, then returning to the center again.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the frame interval value so the clock’s pendulum is swinging at an appropriate speed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might the clock sprite be placed on the screen?

❓ What might the frame interval be set to so that the pendulum swings at a proper speed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja is tinkering with the runImageAnimation code, remind them to think about the value they used in the preview window of the animation paint editor. They may choose to use the same value, or run the image animation on screen, and choose a greater or lesser value based on the rate that the animation runs. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Display the clock animation on screen!


Create a new sprite with its image set to the clockImage asset. Place the sprite in the top right corner of the red floor on screen. Code the sprite to animate continuously using the clockAnim asset. 


Click ▶ to test the clock animation, then tinker with the frame interval value until it is swinging at a proper speed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the window sprite on the teal wall above the fireplace?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the window sprite be used for in this project?

❓ Why should the window sprite’s z-property be set to 1?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The window sprite will act as the background layer for a moon animation, showing the dark blue sky and the stars. Its z-property should be set to 1, so that it appears behind the moon animation and window frame, which will be added in the next steps.
steps.instructions:
Add a window sprite to the scene! 


Open the Assets menu and notice the windowBackgroundImage asset that shows an image with a blue sky and white stars. This will serve as the background layer for the window sprite.


Return to the JavaScript editor and create a new sprite, with its image set to the windowBackgroundImage asset. 


Place the window sprite on the teal wall, above the fireplace on screen. Set the window sprite’s z-property to 1, so that it will appear behind the other animation layers.


Click ▶ to see the window sprite displayed on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the marquee tool to move the moon gradually to the top right of the canvas across several frames?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the canvas be resized to 32 x 32?

❓ Where might the moon be placed in each frame to show it gradually moving across the canvas?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the moonAnim animation asset will be placed in front of the window sprite, just placed on the screen. As a result, its canvas size should match that of the window to create a realistic representation of the moon moving across the sky.

💡 Encourage the ninja to duplicate each frame as they create a new one, to keep track of the previous moon’s position so that they can more easily move it slightly up and to the right.
steps.instructions:
Create a rising moon animation using multiple frames in an animation asset!


In the Assets menu, create a new moonAnim animation asset. Resize the canvas to the same size as the window sprite canvas.


Use the circle tool to draw a moon moving from the bottom left of the canvas to the top right across several frames. The moon should be shown partially off screen once it overlaps the bottom left and top right corners.

Click on the Show Previous Frame tool to compare the current frame with the previous frame. 


The animation should also include a blank frame at the beginning and end of its cycle. 


Click to preview the animation as it cycles through the 5 frames then update the position of the moon to show a realistic movement.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a blank moonImage asset then place it on top of the window background?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the canvas of the moonImage asset remain blank?

❓ Where should the moon sprite be placed on the screen?

❓ What might the frame interval be set to so that the moon moves slowly across the window?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The canvas of the moonImage asset should remain blank because the moon animation will be used to display the rotating images on screen. Remind the ninja that the moon sprite should use the same coordinates as the window sprite, so that it appears directly in front of it.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the moon animation should match the movement in real life; the moon moves slowly across the sky, and the frameInterval value should reflect this. Have the ninja test out the animation and tinker with the frameInterval value.

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Use the moon animation asset to animate the window background!


In the Assets menu, create a new moonImage asset with its canvas set to 32 x 32. Leave the canvas blank.


Return to the JavaScript editor, then create a moon sprite with its image set to the moonImage asset. 


Use the same coordinates as the window sprite to position the moon sprite directly on top of the window background. Set the moon sprite’s z-property, so that it appears in front of the window background.


Code the sprite to animate continuously using the moonAnim asset.


Click ▶ to test the moon animation, then tinker with the frame interval value until it is moving at a proper speed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the z properties so that the layers of the window sprite appear in the correct order?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where will the window sprite appear on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that because of the sequence of the code and z-properties of the 3 sprites, the window sprite will appear as the background layer, the moon animation will appear in front of the background, and the windowFrame will appear as the foreground layer.
steps.instructions:
Complete the window image by adding a frame on top!


Open the Assets menu and notice the windowForegroundImage asset that shows a light blue window frame. This will serve as the foreground layer, to be placed on top of the window sprite.


Return to the JavaScript editor and create a new sprite, with its image set to the windowForegroundImage asset. 


Use the same coordinates as the window and moon sprites to position the frame sprite directly on top of the window background and moon animation. Set the window frame sprite’s z-property, so that it appears in front of the moon animation and the window background.


Click ▶ to test how the different layers appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the personSprite asset as the first frame in the idleAnim animation asset?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is an idle animation? Why might it be used in a project?

❓ What other frames might be added to the idleAnim animation asset to show the person sprite idling? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that an idle animation runs when a sprite is not performing any actions (such as walking, running, flying, etc.). An idle animation is often used in games to show that a player is “ready”, but is not currently involved in any actions. This may look like a sprite bobbing up and down, or doing a different type of movement while standing in place.
steps.instructions:
Create an idle animation for the person sprite!


An idle animation runs when a sprite is not performing any actions. This often looks like a sprite bobbing up and down, ready for their next move.


In the Assets menu, open the personSprite image asset. Use Ctrl + A to select, then copy the entire person image. Create a new idleAnim animation asset then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the tools in the animation paint editor to show the person sprite bobbing up and down as they idle?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might the marquee tool be used to make the person sprite appear shorter in the second frame? 

❓ Where might pixels be added and erased to make the person sprite appear to be shrugging?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja can use the marquee tool by clicking above the left side of the person image, then dragging their cursor to encompass the top half of the image and shifting it down by 1 or 2 pixels.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what a shrugging movement might look like in real life (perhaps the shoulders might move or parts of the hair might become less visible) to determine what pixels to add or remove in the third frame.
steps.instructions:
Create multiple frames for the person sprite’s idle animation!


Duplicate the first frame in the idleAnim animation asset 2 times, so that there are 3 frames total.


In the second frame, use the marquee tool to lower the sprite’s head to create a downward bobbing effect. Select the top half of the image, then shift it down by 1 or 2 pixels, covering the existing pixels to make the sprite appear shorter.


In the third frame, use the erase and paint tools to rearrange the pixels in the person sprite’s hair and shoulders to create an upward bobbing effect. Consider lifting some of the hair pixels, raising the shoulders, and/or removing some of the black hair outline.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a person sprite with an idle animation to the room scene?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might the person sprite be placed on screen?

❓ What might the frame interval be set to so that the person sprite idles at a proper speed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja is tinkering with the runImageAnimation code, remind them to think about the value they used in the preview window of the animation paint editor. They may choose to use the same value, or run the image animation on screen, and choose a greater or lesser value based on the rate that the animation runs. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the documentation if they need help animating a sprite with an animation asset in their code.
steps.instructions:
Display the person sprite animation on screen!


Create a new sprite using the personSprite asset. Place the person sprite in the center left of the red floor, in front of the fireplace. Code the sprite to animate continuously using the idleAnim asset. 


Click ▶ to test the idle animation, then tinker with the frame interval value until the sprite is idling at a proper speed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add additional furniture sprites to complete the room scene?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What other furniture sprites might be added to complete the room?

❓ Where might each sprite be placed on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can filter the sprites in the gallery by category, to easily find the furniture sprites.
steps.instructions:
Complete the project by adding other furniture sprites or background details to the room scene!


Use the furniture images in the gallery or draw your own to add finishing touches to the room. 


Place sprites strategically around the room so that they fit where they would naturally be placed, and are not blocking any of the animated sprites.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: A Cozy Evening
subgroups.introduction: Animate several images in a scene to make a room come to life!

validationItems.text: Create custom animation and image sprites for use in the project.
Use a flameAnim asset to animate the torch and fireplace flame sprites at different rates.
Use a clockAnim asset to animate the clock sprite with a swinging pendulum.
Use 3 different layers to display a moon animation asset through a window frame.
Use an idleAnim asset to animate the person sprite.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 7 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using still images to create animation assets. Different frames can be combined in the animation paint editor to animate a sprite’s movement in many different ways. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 7:

badges.title: I Like to Move It, Move It
badges.description: Use a variety of animation techniques to add movement to pixel art images in a project.

badges.title: Take it for a Spin
badges.description: Create animation assets that give the illusion of a sprite rotating or spinning.

badges.title: Boing!
badges.description: Create animation assets using squash and stretch that give the illusion of a sprite bouncing.

badges.title: Loafin’ Around
badges.description: Create an idle animation for a sprite.

badges.title: Frame by Frame
badges.description: Create animation assets that mimic the realistic movement of objects.

badges.title: It’s Alive!
badges.description: Use different layers to display an animation asset between 2 image assets.
